plans: Wire-first reproduction then origin-based repair: stand up a loopback TLS origin with a self-signed certificate for one fixed hostname plus a header-logging plaintext target; first prove the leak at wire level (a same-hostname secure-to-plaintext 302 forwards the Authorization header in the vulnerable copy), then apply the minimal repair in the redirect-auth rebuild step so credentials are kept only when scheme, hostname and effective port are identical, substituting the implicit default ports 80/443 when omitted and leaving the netrc re-lookup untouched. Finally run a keep/strip regression matrix on both copies: same-origin plaintext and secure keep, cross-host strip, same-host port change strip, explicit versus implicit default ports, 307/308 method and body integrity, and the netrc interaction.

Predicate-first: skip the end-to-end fixture initially and drive the redirect-auth rebuild routine directly with hand-built prepared objects and minimal fake response objects across a URL decision table (scheme x host x port); pin down the current keep/strip behavior and the intended one, derive the smallest predicate change, apply it to a patched working copy, and only afterwards build one end-to-end fixture as confirmation. Risk to manage: faked objects miss the URL-rewrite and history steps that run before the routine, so the in-memory table may not equal wire behavior.

Transport interception: keep the library byte-identical and subclass the adapter layer to log the final request line, Host header and Authorization header at send time for every hop of a redirect chain; map wire-level ground truth for each redirect class, then repair the redirect-auth step and re-run the same interception harness hop by hop. Higher setup cost than the other routes; the value is proving that the rebuild decision is what the transport actually sends.
